title: Cyril and Methodius (9th century)
hook: brothers who made an alphabet so Slavs could pray in their own tongue

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mount Athos, where monks pray for the world before dawn. Your line was the garden of the Mother of God.
screen: `THE GARDEN OF THE MOTHER OF GOD.`

segments.voice: A message arrives in Constantinople from a Slavic prince far to the north. His people have heard Christian preachers, he says, but in languages they don't understand. Send us a teacher who can explain the faith in our own words. The emperor turns to two brothers from Thessalonica who grew up hearing Slavic spoken around them: one a scholar, the other an experienced administrator turned monk. There's one problem. The Slavs have no letters, and you can't hand someone a Gospel in a language nobody has ever written down. Today, Cyril and Methodius.
screen: `A PRINCE ASKS FOR A TEACHER.` → `TWO BROTHERS FROM THESSALONICA.` → `A LANGUAGE WITH NO LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Our account is the old Slavonic life of the younger brother, who was called Constantine; he took the name Cyril only near the end, as a monk. When the request came, the life says, Constantine prayed, and God showed him the letters. He made an alphabet and began to translate, and the first words he wrote were the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God: and the Word was God." The brothers went north and taught in the Slavic language. They translated the Gospels and the prayers of the liturgy, so people could hear the Mass in their own speech. Not everyone liked it. Some clergy, the life says, argued that God could be praised only in three languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Constantine answered with verse after verse of scripture. One psalm, in the Douay-Rheims, says, "Let every spirit praise the Lord." Every spirit, not three languages. The brothers traveled to the pope, who welcomed them and blessed their Slavonic books. Cyril died in Rome. Methodius went back north as a bishop, and through hard years the work went on, after he was gone, in the hands of their students. Catholic and Orthodox Christians both honor the two as saints, and John Paul the Second named them patrons of Europe, together with Benedict. For the brothers, the Gospel was meant to reach people in the words they already spoke.
screen: `GOD SHOWED HIM THE LETTERS.` · `IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.` · `NOT ONLY THREE LANGUAGES.` · `BLESSED IN ROME.` · then, large: `IN THEIR OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone near you whose first language isn't yours, a neighbor, a coworker, a grandparent, and a word they'd love to hear from you: hello, thank you, peace. Breathe slowly and say it quietly a few times, getting the sounds right, standing for a moment inside another tongue. If you pray, thank God for the language you first prayed in, or first heard love in.
Cyril. The monk, born Constantine, who made an alphabet for the Slavs and translated the Gospels with his brother Methodius. Today's word.
Your line: in their own tongue. A whole alphabet, made so a people could hear. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics and Orthodox Christians keep a feast of Saints Cyril and Methodius, and some Slavic churches, Catholic and Orthodox, still celebrate the liturgy in Church Slavonic, the language the brothers wrote down.

chat.says: Why did Cyril and Methodius make a whole new alphabet?
options: The Slavs had no letters; the brothers wanted the Gospel in their own speech.
So Slavic scholars could read Hebrew, Greek and Latin more easily.
To keep their translations hidden from the pope and his clergy.
chat.meaning: The Slavs had no written letters, so Constantine made an alphabet, and the brothers translated the Gospels and liturgy into Slavic.

Slavonic.meaning: the old written language of the Slavs

Methodius.meaning: Cyril's brother, who went back north as a bishop

Cyril.meaning: the name Constantine took as a monk

Constantinople.meaning: the emperor's city, where the request arrived

notes: Vita Constantini 14: Rastislav's request; Constantine prays, God reveals the letters, he begins with John 1:1. Ch. 16: the Venice dispute with the 'trilingual' clergy, where he cites Psalm 150:6 among other texts. Paraphrased; confirm chapters.
Psalm 150:6 in Douay-Rheims reads 'Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia.' Quote omits 'Alleluia'. Confirm.
Methodius described as an administrator (governor of a Slavic district per the Vita Methodii) turned monk; confirm.

The alphabet they made is generally identified with Glagolitic; Cyrillic is later and named after Cyril. Not stated in voice; no 'original' given because the Glagolitic spelling could not be verified here.

Pope Hadrian II blessing the Slavonic books, Cyril's death in Rome, Methodius returning as archbishop: confirm. 'Hard years' alludes to Methodius's imprisonment and later suppression of the Slavonic liturgy in Moravia.
'Many Slavic churches, Catholic and Orthodox' still using Church Slavonic: confirm wording under the claims rule.
John Paul II named them co-patrons of Europe with Benedict (Egregiae Virtutis); year omitted. Confirm.
Outline title says 9th century; not used in voice.
